title: Ezra 4:7–16
context: Under Artaxerxes, opponents write to the king (4:7), and Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the scribe send a letter against Jerusalem (4:8–16). The text says the letter was written in Syrian; from 4:8 through 6:18 the book itself is written in Aramaic in the original. The senders name themselves with a long list of peoples settled in Samaria and beyond the River by Osnappar, a ruler not named in 2 Kings 17, whom many readers identify with an Assyrian king (4:9–10). Their letter warns that the Jews are rebuilding a rebellious city and its walls, that tribute will cease, and that royal records will confirm Jerusalem’s past rebellions (4:11–16). Unlike 4:1–5, this letter concerns the city and its walls rather than the temple, which is one reason many readers take 4:6–23 as a grouping of later opposition placed here by theme; compare the broken walls of Nehemiah 1:3. Readers also differ on whether 4:7 and 4:8 describe one letter or two. This commentary describes the sequence as the text gives it, without fixing it to a reconstructed timeline. Both traditions read the letter as a sober portrait of political accusation and see God ruling over royal courts and their records.

verses.text: In the days of Artaxerxes, Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel, and the rest of his companions wrote to Artaxerxes king of Persia; and the writing of the letter was written in Syrian and delivered in the Syrian language.
verses.arminianNotes: In the days of Artaxerxes, Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel, and their companions write to the king in the Syrian language. Arminian readers note that opposition now works through official channels and written appeals, and that believers must be ready to live faithfully even when their reputation is shaped by others in places they cannot reach.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the shift to royal correspondence as another stage in a conflict that God oversees, since the kings who receive these letters are themselves under his hand (Proverbs 21:1). Shared ground: both traditions read the notice of the letter and its language simply as part of the record, and neither builds doctrine on who these writers were beyond what the text says.

verses.text: Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes the king as follows.
verses.arminianNotes: Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the scribe write a letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes. Arminian readers observe that the narrative preserves the opponents’ own words, letting their case be heard, and they draw from this the call to answer accusations with integrity rather than with retaliation (compare 1 Peter 2:12).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God’s purposes for Jerusalem are carried forward even through records written to stop them, since the very letters of the opponents become part of the account of his faithfulness. Shared ground: both traditions read the letter as real political pressure on a vulnerable community and both see the LORD as sovereign over its outcome.

verses.text: Then Rehum the chancellor, Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of their companions, the Dinaites, and the Apharsathchites, the Tarpelites, the Apharsites, the Archevites, the Babylonians, the Shushanchites, the Dehaites, the Elamites,
verses.arminianNotes: The senders list themselves with many peoples: Dinaites, Apharsathchites, Tarpelites, Apharsites, Archevites, Babylonians, Shushanchites, Dehaites, and Elamites. Arminian readers note that this broad coalition shows how isolated the small returned community was, and that its faithfulness required courage in the face of many neighbors united against it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the list of peoples the wider world that God rules, all of whom are under his hand even when they unite against his people. Shared ground: both traditions read the long list as emphasizing the scale of opposition, and both avoid speculating beyond the text about the exact identity or homeland of each group named.

verses.text: and the rest of the nations whom the great and noble Osnappar brought over and settled in the city of Samaria, and in the rest of the country beyond the River, and so forth, wrote.
verses.arminianNotes: The senders add the rest of the nations whom the great and noble Osnappar settled in Samaria and the country beyond the River. Arminian readers note that these peoples were themselves displaced by empire, and they read the opponents as people with their own history and interests rather than simply as enemies to be scorned.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the movements of whole peoples by imperial decree as part of the history God governs, recalling 2 Kings 17:24, where the king of Assyria who resettles peoples in Samaria is not named. Shared ground: both traditions note that the text names Osnappar here and Esar Haddon at 4:2 without resolving how they relate, and neither treats that question as theologically decisive.

verses.text: This is the copy of the letter that they sent: To King Artaxerxes, from your servants, the people beyond the River.
verses.arminianNotes: The letter opens: to King Artaxerxes, from his servants, the people beyond the River. Arminian readers notice the language of loyal service the senders use, and they observe that appeals to a ruler’s interests can be framed in pious or loyal terms while serving to block another people’s good work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the opponents present themselves as the king’s faithful servants, but the narrative has already shown what they intend, reminding readers that God weighs motives that human rulers cannot see. Shared ground: both traditions read the opening as a reminder that formal courtesy and real fairness are not the same, and that God judges rightly.

verses.text: Be it known to the king that the Jews who came up from you have come to us to Jerusalem. They are building the rebellious and bad city, and have finished the walls and repaired the foundations.
verses.arminianNotes: The senders claim the Jews are building the rebellious and bad city, finishing the walls and repairing the foundations. Arminian readers note that the charge mixes history and accusation, and that God’s people must often live with descriptions of themselves that are partly true about the past yet unfair to their present intentions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the accusation as an attempt to turn Jerusalem’s past against its future, while God has already promised and begun its restoration. Shared ground: both traditions note that the letter speaks of the city and its walls, not the temple, and both read its description as the opponents’ framing rather than a neutral report; how far the walls had progressed is not stated elsewhere in this chapter.

verses.text: Be it known now to the king that if this city is built and the walls finished, they will not pay tribute, custom, or toll, and in the end it will be hurtful to the kings.
verses.arminianNotes: The senders warn that if the city is built, tribute, custom, and toll will stop and the kings will be harmed. Arminian readers observe that the appeal is to the king’s financial self-interest, and they note that opposition to God’s work often presents itself as prudent concern for order, revenue, and stability.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the appeal to tribute the way earthly powers measure everything by their own interests, while God’s purposes for his people move on a different plane. Shared ground: both traditions read the charge as a political argument designed to alarm the king, and both affirm that believers should be good citizens while trusting God rather than rulers for their security.

verses.text: Now because we eat the salt of the palace and it is not appropriate for us to see the king’s dishonor, therefore we have sent and informed the king,
verses.arminianNotes: The senders say they eat the salt of the palace and cannot bear to see the king’s dishonor. Arminian readers take this phrase, commonly understood as an expression of obligation to the king, as a claim of loyalty that gives their warning weight, and they note how loyalty language can be used to justify hostility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the contrast between the senders’ loyalty to an earthly throne and the community’s loyalty to the LORD, whose honor is the real concern of the book. Shared ground: both traditions read the phrase as the senders’ own presentation of their motives, and both avoid overreading it beyond its plain sense of owing service to the king.

verses.text: that search may be made in the book of the records of your fathers. You will see in the book of the records, and know that this city is a rebellious city, and hurtful to kings and provinces, and that they have started rebellions within it in the past. That is why this city was destroyed.
verses.arminianNotes: The senders urge a search of the records to show that Jerusalem rebelled in the past, which is why it was destroyed. Arminian readers note that Scripture itself records Jerusalem’s rebellion against Babylon (2 Kings 24:20; 2 Chronicles 36:13), so the charge has a basis, though it leaves out the community’s present purpose.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Scripture presents the destruction ultimately as the LORD’s judgment on persistent unfaithfulness (2 Chronicles 36:15–17), something the senders’ political reading cannot see. Shared ground: both traditions read the charge as a partial truth used against a restored people, and both see God as the one who both judged Jerusalem and now restores it.

verses.text: We inform the king that if this city is built and the walls finished, then you will have no possession beyond the River.
verses.arminianNotes: The letter closes with the warning that if the city is built the king will lose his possession beyond the River. Arminian readers see deliberate exaggeration meant to provoke a quick decision, and they note how fear can be used to move those in power against people who pose no real threat.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the senders overstate the danger posed by a small community, while the real power over the region belongs to the LORD, who gives kingdoms to whom he wills. Shared ground: both traditions read the closing warning as rhetoric aimed at the king’s fears, and both see that the narrative invites readers to judge the letter by what they already know of the returned exiles.
